AI Learning Lab — Architect's analysis

The spec proposes a walk-forward portfolio simulator with model versioning, MIT bucket learning, and macro-season testing. This doc lays out what's strong, what's unrealistic for Helm's current architecture, what to incorporate, and — critically — what it does not touch in the existing engine.
Architect's review · Jun 2026
Verdict

What it is

A walk-forward backtester + model versioning registry. The core idea is sound: run the existing model on historical data, measure it honestly, propose rule tweaks, test them out-of-sample, accept or reject. This is exactly what Phase 4 (A-Light learning loop) is scaffolded for.

What it isn't

It's not an AI in the generative sense — it's deterministic rule-based simulation + KPI evaluation. Sections calling it "AI Learning" are marketing language. The actual mechanism is: run rules on history, score them, tweak, repeat. That's honest and achievable.

Realism check

The spec assumes a backend server, 20 SQL tables, background job queues, 300 assets with 5yr history, and 7 separate engines. Helm is a static HTML app. That gap matters. We don't discard the ideas — we adapt the architecture.

Pros & cons of the spec

Strengths — what the spec gets right

  • Walk-forward methodology is correct. Oldest 50% train, newest 50% out-of-sample, day-by-day, no future leakage. This is the only honest way to validate a signal.
  • Model versioning is excellent. v0.1.0 Base → incremental versions → rollback. Exactly what A-Light needs to graduate from "proposed" to "accepted."
  • MIT bucket × macro regime scoring matrix (section 9) is immediately usable — it maps directly onto regime.jsx and plan.jsx already built.
  • Acceptance/rejection rules are rigorous. Sharpe +5%, drawdown doesn't worsen, multi-asset validation, regime diversity. Prevents overfitting a single ticker.
  • Improvement log format (section 16) is excellent — the structured "Finding / Proposed improvement / Result / Decision" format is ready to adopt into the Learning tab today.
  • KPI hierarchy is correct. Risk-adjusted return (Sharpe/Sortino/Calmar) ranks above raw CAGR. Turnover and fees are first-class. This matches Helm's institutional scorecard.
  • Learning Controller Stop/Pause/Reset/Rollback matches A-Light's manual-approval philosophy exactly.
  • MVP phase plan is pragmatic. Start with 5–15 tickers, one risk model, daily simulation. Scale later. Don't build 300 assets first.
  • Anti-overfitting controls are well-designed: multi-asset, multi-regime, multi-time-window validation before acceptance.

Weaknesses — what the spec gets wrong

  • Architecture mismatch. The spec assumes a backend (20 SQL tables, job queues, API endpoints, incremental imports). Helm is a static single-file HTML app. That's a different product category.
  • 300-asset daily simulation is not browser-feasible. 300 assets × 5 years × 252 days = ~378,000 daily simulation steps × scoring logic = browser lockup. Needs a Web Worker at minimum.
  • Massively redundant with Helm. Macro Seasons Engine = regime.jsx (done). MIT buckets = plan.jsx (done). Risk models = strategy.jsx (done). Learning tab = learning.jsx (done). The spec reinvents all of these.
  • Data dependency is unsolved. Historical daily OHLCV for 300 assets requires a proper data pipeline. Our feed has ~109 tickers at EOD. The spec doesn't provide the data — it just assumes it's there.
  • "AI Learning" is misleading branding. There is no neural network, no gradient descent, no parameter update. It's rule engineering + backtesting. That's fine — but calling it an "AI Learning Lab" overstates what it does and risks false confidence.
  • LLM overuse in the simulation loop. The spec suggests using Claude for summarizing findings, proposing changes, writing logs — but warns against calling LLM per-day/ticker. The boundary is underspecified and could get expensive.
  • Sections 20–22 (DB schema, backend APIs, background jobs) are irrelevant for Helm's static architecture. They describe a SaaS product, not an HTML prototype.
  • Crypto High Conviction risk model (75% crypto max) in a research/simulation tool is dangerous — it could generate misleading "improvements" that only work in bull markets.
  • Transaction import complexity (Mode A: reconstruct from buy/sell dates, FX, fees, dividends) is a large separate project and not essential for the MVP value.
Gate impact — what changes in the existing engine?
✓ Zero gate changes
The spec explicitly prohibits modifying the existing engine. It is registered as v0.1.0 and runs as-is forever as the baseline.

The Learning Lab is a sandboxed parallel environment. It calls the existing signalsFor(), scoreFamilies(), and classifyRegime() functions as read-only oracles — the baseline it measures against. Candidate improvements are tested inside the simulator only. Nothing reaches the live Strategy Lab, Cockpit, or Screener until you manually approve it via the Learning tab's existing A-Light proposal flow.

strategy.jsx / signalsFor()
No change — becomes v0.1.0
Called by the simulator as the baseline model. Output is compared vs candidate; never overwritten automatically.
regime.jsx / classifyRegime()
No change — feeds the simulator
Already classifies growth × inflation → season. Simulator reads HelmRegime to tag each simulated trade with the macro season at that date.
plan.jsx / bucketOf()
No change — MIT mapping already exists
The spec's "MIT bucket" = Helm's "Volatile Offense / Satellite / Core Growth / Ballast" structure. Already computed. The scoring matrix (+2/+1/0/-1/-2) extends it, not replaces it.
learning.jsx / reflexion ledger
Extended, not replaced
The existing A-Light ledger (predicted vs realized, drift, proposals) becomes the receiver for simulator output. The log format from section 16 of the spec slots directly into the existing improvement log structure.
What I'd incorporate — prioritized
1

Walk-forward engine (MVP: 15 tickers, Web Worker)

Runs the existing signalsFor() day-by-day on a 2yr price history split 50/50. Records predicted direction vs actual close. Stores to helm_sim_v1 localStorage. Runs in a Web Worker so the UI stays live. This is the core value of the entire spec.
Phase 1 MVP. Uses existing signals engine as v0.1.0 baseline. No new data sources needed beyond what the feed already provides.
Build first
2

Model version registry

v0.1.0 = current signalsFor(). Every accepted tweak to factor weights, buy bar, or RSI thresholds creates a new version with full KPI before/after. Stored in localStorage. The existing Learning tab already shows proposals — version registry is the missing upgrade.
Extends learning.jsx. The "accepted improvements" flow already exists. Adds version numbering, rollback, and diff view.
Build first
3

MIT bucket × macro season scoring matrix

The spec's section 9 (+2/+1/0/-1/-2 per regime per bucket) is immediately valuable and can be a static table that the simulator tests against historical regime classifications. Ties directly into regime.jsx's season work.
New section in regime.jsx or plan.jsx. Already have the 4-season framework — this adds the asset-class performance expectations the spec formalizes.
Build first
4

Improvement log (spec's section 16 format)

Adopt the structured log format: Finding / Proposed improvement / Result / Decision / Reason. Replace the current plain-text proposals in learning.jsx with this richer format. Every accepted or rejected change is permanently logged.
Minor extension to learning.jsx proposals section. The data structure already exists in A-Light — this just formalizes the schema.
Build first
5

KPI comparison table (candidate vs baseline vs benchmarks)

The simulator's output surface: existing model vs candidate vs buy-and-hold vs benchmark, with Sharpe / Sortino / Calmar / max DD / turnover / fees. Acceptance/rejection rules shown explicitly. Central to the spec's value.
New section inside the Learning tab (or Backtest tab). Simulated, not live — clearly labelled as research only.
Phase 2
6

Learning Controller (Start/Pause/Stop/Reset/Rollback)

UI controls for the simulation: Quick Test (15 tickers, 3 iterations), Medium (50 tickers, 10 iterations), Full (needs confirmation). Run progress, elapsed time, current asset, accepted/rejected counters.
New "Learning Lab" section. Could replace Backtest tab or extend it.
Phase 2
7

Portfolio equity curve comparison

AI-managed sim vs baseline vs buy-and-hold plotted over the out-of-sample period. Uses the Catmull-Rom chart already in charts.jsx. Drawdown curve alongside.
Extends charts.jsx. Data comes from the walk-forward engine snapshots stored in localStorage.
Phase 2
8

Return by macro regime / MIT bucket heatmap

How did each risk model perform in Spring vs Summer vs Fall vs Winter? Which MIT bucket had the best/worst regime fit? This is the spec's most unique analytical value.
Phase 3, after walk-forward engine is running and generating enough trade history to slice by regime.
Phase 3
What to skip — and why
Spec sectionWhy skipAlternative in Helm
Backend DB (20 tables, SQL) Helm is a static HTML app with no server. A 20-table SQL schema requires infrastructure that doesn't exist and contradicts the zero-cost architecture. localStorage + JSON. Enough for 30-snapshot journals, version history, and sim results for a solo investor. Add IndexedDB if data grows.
Background job queues / API endpoints No backend = no job queues. These are a SaaS architecture concern, not a single-user browser app. Web Worker for simulation (non-blocking, runs in background, posts progress messages to UI — same user experience).
300-asset universe import No free source of 300× daily OHLCV at the resolution needed. The feed has ~109 positions EOD. Adding 300 requires a paid data vendor. Use the 109 held positions + Screener universe (47 names already seeded). Cap MVP at ~30 tickers. Scale with the feed as it grows.
Mode A: transaction reconstruction Reconstructing portfolio value from every buy/sell/dividend/FX/deposit transaction is a large separate project. You'd need full NBDB transaction exports and a reconciliation engine. Mode B (current holdings backcast) is simpler and gives 90% of the analytical value for discovering model weaknesses.
Crypto High Conviction risk model (75% crypto) A model that recommends 75% crypto during a bull market backtest will always look good — it's selection bias built into the risk preset. Dangerous for validation. Use the existing 3 risk models (Conservative/Balanced/Aggressive). The Aggressive model at 30% volatile-offense cap is already aggressive enough.
"AI" branding throughout The mechanism is deterministic rule-based backtesting, not machine learning. Calling it AI creates false confidence in results. Call it "Walk-Forward Simulator" or "Strategy Validator." Reserve "AI" label for the actual Claude calls that summarize findings and write the improvement log.
Impact on existing Helm files — the full map
strategy.jsx
No changes. signalsFor() and scoreFamilies() become the v0.1.0 baseline. The simulator calls them as read-only oracles and compares candidates against their output. Never overwritten automatically.
No change
regime.jsx
No changes. classifyRegime() is used by the simulator to tag each simulated trade with the macro season. The MIT × season scoring matrix (section 9 of spec) gets added as a new read-only static table — not a change to the classifier.
No change
learning.jsx
Extended. The improvement log format is upgraded to the spec's structured schema (Finding / Proposed change / KPI before/after / Decision). The reflexion ledger gains a "from simulator" source tag. The version registry panel is added. Core A-Light logic unchanged.
Extend only
backtest.jsx
Extended or replaced by the new Learning Lab module. Current backtest is a deterministic curve on your holdings. The simulator adds the walk-forward, version comparison, and candidate model testing on top. Existing backtest chart is reused inside the new UI.
Extend only
plan.jsx
No changes. The "Volatile Offense / Satellite / Core Growth / Ballast" bucket structure is Helm's MIT equivalent. The simulator reads bucketOf(h) to tag trades. No modifications to Plan or the funded-ratio engine.
No change
screener.jsx
No changes. window.HelmUniverse is already exposed. The simulator reads it as the candidate universe for buy signals. The Screener UI itself doesn't change.
No change
app.jsx nav
Minor. "Backtest" in the Understand group is renamed or expanded to "Strategy Validator" once the new module is built. One label change, same route.
Label only
Proposed build phases
Phase 1
Walk-forward MVP
  • 15 tickers (your held names)
  • Existing model as v0.1.0
  • 2yr history from feed
  • 50/50 train/test split
  • Day-by-day signal replay
  • Predicted vs realized log
  • Stop/Reset controls
  • Basic KPI (Sharpe, DD, win rate)
Phase 2
Version registry + KPI table
  • Model version registry (v0.1.0 baseline)
  • Candidate vs baseline KPI table
  • Acceptance/rejection logic
  • Structured improvement log
  • Equity curve comparison chart
  • Rollback to previous version
Phase 3
MIT + macro season analysis
  • MIT × macro scoring matrix
  • Return by regime / bucket heatmap
  • Regime tagging on every trade
  • Drawdown by MIT bucket
  • Best/worst regime per bucket
Phase 4
Scale + full controller
  • 50+ tickers (Screener universe)
  • Multiple risk models
  • Web Worker (non-blocking)
  • Quick / Medium / Full run modes
  • Claude for improvement log writing
  • Anti-overfitting validation
The spec's 1,481 lines contain real engineering wisdom. The right move is to extract the methodology (walk-forward, versioning, acceptance rules, log format) and adapt it to Helm's actual architecture — not implement the spec as written. The existing engine is untouched. The lab is a sandboxed research surface that feeds proposals back to you for manual approval.
